issues.legal_issue: A buyer’s failure to complete a sale by the original deadline does not defeat a specific-performance claim where the seller later revived or extended the agreement and the seller’s own outstanding obligations prevented completion.
material_facts: The buyer made substantial part-payments, demanded completion, and stated that she was ready and willing to perform her obligations.
The seller did not produce the original title documents or redeem the mortgage when required for completion.
After the original completion period, the seller sought an extension and accepted further payments from the buyer.
The seller had accepted the buyer’s position that the sale would be completed by a later date.
issues.conclusion: The buyer’s failure to complete by the original deadline did not defeat the claim; the seller had waived reliance on that deadline by reviving the agreement and seeking an extension, and the seller’s own outstanding obligations also prevented completion.
issues.legal_principle: In a specific-performance suit, the plaintiff must establish readiness and willingness, but whether that burden is met depends on the circumstances of the case and has no rigid formula. Readiness and willingness are assessed in light of what the defendant was required to do under the agreement. A seller who later revives or extends the agreement cannot rely on the earlier deadline as a bar. Ardeshir H. Mama v. Flora Sassoon was distinguished because it concerned the absence of a completed contract.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a claim by a buyer for specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.buyer_demonstrated_readiness: The buyer made payments or otherwise acted to show willingness and ability to perform the buyer’s obligations.
predicates.seller_failed_completion_obligations: The seller did not perform an obligation needed to enable completion, such as clearing an encumbrance or producing required title documents.
predicates.seller_later_revived_or_extended_agreeme: After the original completion period, the seller treated the agreement as continuing by seeking an extension or accepting further performance.

issues.definition: When a buyer seeking specific performance demonstrates readiness and the seller either fails to perform necessary completion obligations or later treats the agreement as continuing, the original deadline does not bar the claim.

issues.legal_issue: A clause providing for a payment on breach does not bar specific performance unless the contract gives the defaulting party an option to pay that amount instead of performing.
material_facts: The agreement required the seller to discharge the mortgage and provided for return of the advance and liquidated damages if the seller breached and failed to sell.
The clause did not state that the seller could elect to pay the specified amount instead of conveying the property.
The buyer sought specific performance despite the clause.
issues.conclusion: The damages clause did not make the specific-performance suit unmaintainable; it secured performance rather than giving the seller an option to substitute payment for the sale.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits specific performance where a sum is named for breach if the sum secures performance rather than giving the defaulting party an option to pay money in lieu of performance. M.L. Devender Singh v. Syed Khaja distinguishes a security or damages stipulation from a contractual alternative to performance and treats the stated sum as evidence, not a conclusive answer. Manzoor Ahmed Magray v. Gulam Hassan Aram and A. Abdul Rashid Khan v. P.A.K.A. Shahul Hamid reiterate that approach. Dadarao v. Ramrao was distinguished and held per incuriam because it did not consider Section 23 or the earlier binding decision in M.L. Devender Singh.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and contract_contains_breach_payment_clause and clause_secures_performance and not seller_has_payment_instead_option

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a claim by a buyer for specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.contract_contains_breach_payment_clause: The agreement specifies a payment or repayment consequence if a party breaches it.
predicates.clause_secures_performance: The payment consequence is intended to secure performance or compensate for breach rather than define an alternative performance.
predicates.seller_has_payment_instead_option: The agreement expressly allows the seller to choose payment instead of conveying the property.

issues.definition: If a specific-performance claim concerns an agreement with a breach-payment clause that secures performance and gives the seller no payment-instead option, that clause does not bar specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: An increase in property value during the period before enforcement does not, by itself, justify refusing specific performance or requiring a higher payment.
material_facts: The seller accepted part-payments from the buyer over time and accepted a further substantial payment shortly before the suit was filed.
The seller redeemed the mortgage after receiving the required payment from the buyer.
The seller’s hardship argument based on increased property prices had not been raised before the High Court.
The buyer would also suffer hardship if the agreement were not performed.
issues.conclusion: The increase in property prices did not justify denying the buyer the benefit of specific performance in the circumstances of the case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary, and the court must consider the circumstances, including unfair advantage and hardship. Explanation I to Section 20 provides that inadequacy of consideration or an onerous or improvident bargain, by itself, does not constitute unfair advantage. Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation does not establish an absolute rule that escalation in property prices requires refusal of specific performance or an increased payment; the result depends on the circumstances of each case.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and property_value_increased and seller_accepted_buyer_performance and buyer_would_suffer_from_nonperformance

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a claim by a buyer for specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.property_value_increased: The value of the property rose between the agreement and the court’s consideration of enforcement.
predicates.seller_accepted_buyer_performance: The seller accepted payments or other performance from the buyer while the agreement remained in issue.
predicates.buyer_would_suffer_from_nonperformance: The buyer would face hardship if the agreement were not performed.

issues.definition: When property value has risen but the seller accepted the buyer’s performance and the buyer would suffer from nonperformance, the rise alone does not justify refusing specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: A factual finding that a buyer was ready and willing to perform is binding on further appeal when no material error in the finding is shown.
material_facts: The High Court found on the evidence that the buyer had been ready and willing to perform her obligations.
The appellant did not show that the High Court relied on an irrelevant fact or failed to consider a relevant fact.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s factual finding on readiness and willingness was binding in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Whether the plaintiff discharged the burden of proving readiness and willingness depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. A factual finding by the High Court is binding on further appeal where the appellant has not shown that the finding rests on an irrelevant consideration or omits a relevant one.

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a claim for specific performance.
predicates.high_court_found_buyer_ready: The High Court made a factual finding that the buyer was ready and willing to perform.
predicates.no_material_error_shown: The appellant did not show that the High Court relied on irrelevant material or ignored relevant material.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance appeal, a High Court finding that the buyer was ready and willing is binding when no material error in that finding is shown.
